## Active

### D-149 — The leg id is a library concept, not something hop() invents

> _2026-09-14 · core/semantic-log · active_

The owner ruling, made before implementation: leg ids should be native to semantic-log, not bound
only to the `hop()` function, since that is just a demo. The library therefore owns the binder, the
id's charset, the propagation convention and the requirement behind it, and `hop()` is one consumer
of the identity rather than its author. The same reasoning moved `readIdentity()` onto the public
surface: the propagation contract is enforced on the way out by `identityHeaders()` and on the way
in by the rule that a comma-joined duplicate header is not an identity, and leaving the inbound half
to each application meant one subtle rule re-implemented per application. Verified with 2303 of 2303
tap tests at 100% coverage, up from 2258, and a clean lint.

### D-150 — A leg is a scope bound around a call, not a hop parameter

> _2026-09-14 · core/semantic-log · active_

The plan had `hop()` taking a required `{leg}` option; it is implemented as `bindLeg(id, fn)`
wrapping the call, because the caller's own request-describing records are emitted immediately
before the hop and, with the id bound only inside `hop()`, those records would carry no leg — the
cross-reference the feature exists for would be missing exactly where a reader looks first. `hop()`
still throws when no leg is bound, so an id cannot be forgotten silently: what changed is where the
id is declared, not whether one is required. The ambient context keeps the leg beside the flow and
the logger joins the two when it assembles a record (`flowWithLeg`), because replacing the flow
object at bind time would have detached `step`'s position from the enclosing scope, an object
deliberately shared by reference with every nested scope. Reconsider if a call site needs a leg on
the wire but not on its own records.

### D-151 — The leg id charset is the one that survives all four consumers

> _2026-09-14 · core/semantic-log · active_

The enforced charset is lowercase letters and digits plus `.`, `-` and `_`, chosen because one
charset has to survive four consumers at once: an HTTP header value, a source grep for the
id-to-file cross-reference, a diagram label needing no escaping, and the `;` that silently breaks a
generated sequence diagram.

### D-152 — A hop is observed at both ends, and the rule is documented

> _2026-09-14 · core/semantic-log · active_

This was taken autonomously, with the owner away and instructing to proceed and make good decisions.
A hop is two observations of one leg id, because a leg id names a call site and encodes no endpoint:
the caller's record, emitted inside the leg scope, and the callee's receipt, emitted under the
inbound leg. The owner was offered (A) instrument both ends and document the rule, (B) propagate the
caller's service name as a fourth identity, or (C) infer the caller from leg order, and (A) was
taken. The fixture now logs the request inside each leg and a receipt under the inbound leg, which
added nine protocol records: three receipts, from the hub `/parties`, hubA `/parties` and the proxy,
and six requests, covering hub to fxp quotes, hub to payee quotes and transfers, hubA to fxpA
quotes, and hubA to proxy quotes and transfers. The rationale is that the topology stays a fact at
both ends, the identity model stays as ruled with three headers and neutral ids, and a hop nobody
logged loses its edge visibly instead of inventing one. Reconsider if the lighter contract is wanted
for real applications: (B) costs one more header and needs only one observation, while (C) costs
nothing but makes the topology an inference that is wrong when hops interleave.

### D-153 — The observed-call union is written with the batch, not debounced

> _2026-09-14 · core/semantic-log · active_

The original ruling said the per-kind union of observed calls is written on a debounce with a flush
on close, with the window as a named option. It was implemented and then removed, because the window
buys nothing: the unions live in the same snapshot file as the template registry, and the durability
requirement says the registry must be on disk before a batch is acknowledged, so the file is already
written once per accepted batch and the union is in it. Debouncing the union half would mean either
writing the file twice per batch, or writing the registry without its unions and then again with
them. What a debounce would add is a window in which observations are not on disk, for a service
whose whole point is that its shape survives a restart. `ServiceOptions.persistDebounceMs` is gone
and the `onClose` flush went with it, since there is never a pending write. Reconsider if the
snapshot ever grows big enough that a per-batch write is a real cost: the answer then is a separate
append-only surface for observations, not a timer.

### D-154 — Diagram lookup is one route, resolved by the reference's shape

> _2026-09-14 · core/semantic-log · active_

The plan named two routes, `GET /flows/:kind/diagram` and `GET /flows/:id/diagram`, but Fastify
cannot register one pattern twice, so they are one route, `GET /flows/:reference/diagram`, and the
reference's shape decides which store is asked: a ULID is an execution, since nothing else parses as
one, and anything else is a kind. The two 404s stay distinct and legible: `unknown flow kind` lists
the kinds there are, and `flow execution not retained` reports how many are held and how many were
evicted.

### D-155 — A closed execution records its status but never refuses observations

> _2026-09-14 · core/semantic-log · active_

This supersedes my own earlier rule that a spent execution takes no further calls. The generated
artifact `docs/observed-flows.md` proved it wrong on the first real run: the payer's sink flushes
before the hub's, so the payer's terminal `transfer complete` reached the service first and the
hub's last four records were refused, losing the hub's own declaration of `hub.transfer.deliver` —
an entire edge of the observed flow — plus three receipts. Arrival order between processes is not
emission order. The terminal status is now recorded as `closed`, a fact about what the emitter
reported, and never refuses an observation; redeliveries are still deduplicated by event id and
retention is still bounded by the cap.
